units.title: Unit 85 — Countable and uncountable nouns with different meanings
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 176–177 (PDF pages 177–178).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish material and abstract mass senses from countable objects and individual occasions.
Use articles and plural forms to contrast glass, paper, hair, iron, experience and other nouns.
Recognise serving senses of drinks and foods, including a coffee and a chocolate.
Explain sense changes in less obvious contrasts such as plant, damage/damages and arts/art.

items.example: The new entrance door is made from toughened glass.
items.note: Uncountable when referring to the material; a glass is a drinking vessel.

items.example: Could you put a clean glass on the table for our guest?
items.note: Countable vessel; two glasses means two drinking vessels.

items.example: They chose a thick cloth for the new curtains.
items.note: Uncountable for fabric in general; contrast with a cloth for cleaning.

items.example: Use a soft cloth to clean the screen.
items.note: A countable piece of fabric, particularly for wiping or cleaning.

items.example: We often eat fish with vegetables on Fridays.
items.note: Uncountable when referring to fish as food.

items.example: A colourful fish swam past the reef.
items.note: A countable animal; the usual plural is fish.

items.example: It will take a lot of work to restore the old building.
items.note: Uncountable for effort and tasks in general; a work can mean a creation.

items.example: The exhibition includes a work by a local sculptor.
items.note: Countable in the sense of an artistic or literary creation.

items.example: She bought a small work of art at the charity auction.
items.note: A countable artistic creation; also used figuratively for something especially well made.

items.example: Her hair became darker as she got older.
items.note: Uncountable when talking about all the hair on a person’s head.

items.pt: um fio de cabelo; um pelo
items.example: I found a hair on my jacket after brushing the dog.
items.note: One individual strand; hairs refers to multiple separate strands.

items.example: We need more paper for the office printer.
items.note: Uncountable as a material used for writing or printing.

items.example: My professor recommended a paper on renewable energy.
items.note: Countable for a newspaper or an academic article, among other uses.

items.example: People from several countries attended the workshop.
items.note: Ordinary plural referring to individual persons.

items.example: The museum describes the traditions of different Indigenous peoples.
items.note: Plural of people in the sense of a nation or ethnic group, not a plural meaning individuals.

items.example: The bridge contains a large amount of iron.
items.note: Uncountable for the metal.

items.example: The hotel can lend you an iron if you need one.
items.note: Countable household appliance used to remove creases.

items.example: She has valuable experience of working with children.
items.note: Uncountable for accumulated practical knowledge or skill.

items.example: Visiting the observatory was an unforgettable experience.
items.note: Countable for one particular event; plural experiences is also common.

items.example: The gallery is dedicated to contemporary art.
items.note: Usually uncountable for visual art, painting, drawing and sculpture.

items.example: The city invests in the arts through festivals and grants.
items.note: Plural expression covering cultural areas such as music, theatre and literature.

items.pt: humanidades; cursos de artes e letras
items.example: He studied arts before training as an engineer.
items.note: As a field of university study, arts commonly includes humanities subjects.

items.example: Time seems to pass more quickly when we are busy.
items.note: Uncountable for time as a continuous concept.

items.example: We have met several times since the conference.
items.note: Countable occasions or periods; good times and bad times describe experiences.

items.example: There was a time when nobody used smartphones.
items.note: Countable for one particular period or occasion.

items.example: There is fresh coffee in the kitchen.
items.note: Uncountable for the drink; a coffee is a serving.

items.pt: um café; uma xícara de café
items.example: I ordered a coffee while waiting for the train.
items.note: A countable serving, usually a cup of coffee.

items.example: He prefers tea without sugar.
items.note: Usually uncountable for the drink; a tea can mean one serving.

items.pt: um chá; uma xícara de chá
items.example: She asked for a tea and a glass of water.
items.note: Countable for a serving; two teas means two servings.

items.example: There was some mashed potato left after lunch.
items.note: Uncountable for potato as a prepared food or substance.

items.example: A large potato is enough for this recipe.
items.note: A countable whole vegetable; plural potatoes.

items.example: The cake contains dark chocolate and almonds.
items.note: Usually uncountable for chocolate as a substance.

items.example: She offered each visitor a chocolate from the box.
items.note: Countable for one chocolate sweet or confection.

items.example: Add a little black pepper to the sauce.
items.note: Uncountable when referring to the ground seasoning.

items.example: He chopped a red pepper for the salad.
items.note: Countable for a pepper vegetable or fruit; the intended variety depends on context.

items.example: Add a little salt and pepper before serving.
items.note: Common combination of seasonings, both normally uncountable as substances.

items.example: The soup needs a little more onion.
items.note: Uncountable when treated as chopped or prepared food.

items.example: Please slice an onion for the sandwiches.
items.note: Countable for one whole onion.

items.example: The old table is made of solid wood.
items.note: Uncountable when referring to timber as a material.

items.example: There is a quiet wood behind the village.
items.note: A countable area of trees; often called woods in the plural.

items.example: The seals are made from flexible rubber.
items.note: Uncountable for the elastic material.

items.example: Can I borrow a rubber to correct my pencil marks?
items.note: British English for an eraser; American English usually says eraser.

items.example: Would you like some cake after dinner?
items.note: Uncountable for a portion of cake.

items.example: He baked a cake for the birthday party.
items.note: Countable for one complete cake.

items.example: The factory invested in modern plant and machinery.
items.note: Uncountable in formal industrial contexts for heavy equipment or production facilities.

items.example: She put a small plant beside the window.
items.note: Countable for one living botanical organism.

items.example: The storm caused significant damage to the roof.
items.note: Normally uncountable for harm or destruction.

items.example: The court ordered the company to pay damages.
items.note: Plural legal noun for money awarded as compensation; not the ordinary plural of damage.

items.example: Relevant work experience is required for this role.
items.note: Experience is uncountable for accumulated job-related knowledge.

items.example: We shared some good times during our university years.
items.note: Plural expression for enjoyable periods or experiences.

units.title: Unit 86 — Making uncountable nouns countable
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 178–179 (PDF pages 179–180).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Form countable expressions with a piece of and a bit of without pluralising mass nouns.
Use specific weather and nature quantity nouns, such as a gust of wind and a flash of lightning.
Choose natural units for groceries, clothing, news and equipment.
Use the fixed pattern a state of with abstract nouns, including flux and disrepair.

sectionsChecked: B: Words that go with specific uncountable nouns
Weather diagram and groceries, nature, and other word groups

items.pt: um pedaço de; uma unidade de
items.example: Could you cut a piece of the material for me?
items.note: Productive partitive pattern; what follows of must be specified in context.

items.example: There is a bit of dust on the desk.
items.note: Informal partitive; often suggests a relatively small amount.

items.example: Each passenger may bring one piece of luggage into the cabin.
items.note: Use piece or item to count luggage; not a luggage.

items.pt: uma informação; um dado de informação
items.example: I found a useful bit of information in the report.
items.note: Less formal than a piece of information; information itself is uncountable.

items.example: The orchestra rehearsed a new piece of music.
items.note: A natural way to count musical compositions.

items.example: Here is a bit of advice for your first day at work.
items.note: An informal way to count advice; a piece of advice is more neutral.

items.example: My teacher gave me a piece of advice about pronunciation.
items.note: Counts one suggestion without treating advice as a countable noun.

items.pt: um equipamento; uma peça de equipamento
items.example: We need one more piece of equipment for the test bench.
items.note: Equipment is uncountable, so count individual items with piece.

items.pt: um equipamento; uma peça de equipamento
items.example: That little bit of equipment is surprisingly expensive.
items.note: A more informal reference to an individual item of equipment.

items.pt: um móvel; uma peça de mobília
items.example: An antique piece of furniture stood near the fireplace.
items.note: Furniture is uncountable; a furniture is incorrect in ordinary use.

items.example: They delivered three pieces of furniture this morning.
items.note: Pluralise the counting word pieces, not furniture.

items.example: A sudden shower of rain interrupted the match.
items.note: A shower is a short period of rain, often rather heavy.

items.example: We waited indoors during a heavy shower.
items.note: Common countable weather noun for a brief period of heavy rain.

items.example: A sunny spell brightened the afternoon.
items.note: Spell describes a period of a particular kind of weather.

items.example: A spell of windy weather delayed the ferry service.
items.note: Spell can quantify an extended period of a weather condition.

items.example: We heard a distant rumble of thunder beyond the hills.
items.note: Rumble describes a low, rolling thunder sound.

items.pt: um relâmpago; um clarão de raio
items.example: A flash of lightning lit up the valley.
items.note: Use flash to count a brief burst of lightning.

items.example: A loud clap of thunder startled the children.
items.note: Clap highlights one sharp thunder sound.

items.pt: um pingo de chuva; um pouco de chuva
items.example: A few spots of rain fell as we left the station.
items.note: A spot is a small amount or drop; often used in the plural for light rain.

items.example: A strong gust of wind blew the door shut.
items.note: Gust is a sudden brief increase in wind speed.

items.pt: um pão inteiro; uma forma de pão
items.example: We bought a loaf of bread from the bakery.
items.note: Loaf counts one whole shaped piece of bread.

items.example: She added a slice of ham to the sandwich.
items.note: Slice counts one thin flat piece.

items.example: He ate a slice of toast before leaving.
items.note: Toast is usually uncountable; use a slice of toast to count servings.

items.example: Can you put a slice of cheese on my sandwich?
items.note: Slice is also natural with bread and meat.

items.example: I shared a bar of chocolate with my sister.
items.note: Bar counts a rectangular block of chocolate.

items.pt: um tubo de pasta de dente
items.example: There is a spare tube of toothpaste in the cupboard.
items.note: Tube measures toothpaste by its container.

items.example: She picked up a carton of milk on the way home.
items.note: Carton is a common container for milk or juice.

items.example: Please leave a new bar of soap by the sink.
items.note: Bar is a natural unit for solid soap.

items.pt: uma folha de grama; uma lâmina de capim
items.example: A single blade of grass was caught in the camera lens.
items.note: Blade counts one thin leaf of grass.

items.example: A dark cloud of smoke rose above the warehouse.
items.note: Cloud describes a large visible mass of smoke.

items.example: A puff of smoke escaped from the chimney.
items.note: Puff refers to a small burst or cloud of smoke.

items.pt: um pouco de ar fresco; uma lufada de ar fresco
items.example: I went outside for a breath of fresh air.
items.note: Both a literal quantity of air and an expression for something refreshing.

items.example: He threw a lump of coal onto the fire.
items.note: Lump counts a solid, often irregular piece.

items.example: Would you like a lump of sugar in your tea?
items.note: Lump can also describe one piece of solid sugar.

items.pt: um golpe de sorte; uma sorte inesperada
items.example: By a stroke of luck, we found the missing key.
items.note: Stroke of luck is a fixed expression for unexpected good fortune.

items.pt: o mínimo de trabalho; um pingo de trabalho
items.example: He has not done a stroke of work all morning.
items.note: Used in negatives to stress complete lack of effort; not a normal affirmative quantity.

items.example: During a fit of temper, he slammed the door.
items.note: A sudden short episode of anger; also a fit of anger.

items.example: Cycling is an inexpensive means of transport.
items.note: Means can be singular or plural without changing form; one means, two means.

items.example: Every article of clothing had a name tag.
items.note: A somewhat formal way to refer to one garment.

items.example: She donated an item of clothing to the shelter.
items.note: Item counts one garment; also an article of clothing.

items.example: One interesting item of news concerned the new railway.
items.note: News is uncountable, so item identifies one report or piece of information.

items.example: The office was in a state of chaos after the move.
items.note: Chaos is an abstract uncountable noun describing extreme disorder.

items.example: The negotiations ended in a state of tension.
items.note: A period or situation marked by strained relations or anxiety.

items.example: The conflicting instructions left everyone in a state of confusion.
items.note: Confusion means uncertainty about what is happening or what to do.

items.example: The doctor assessed his general state of health.
items.note: Health is uncountable; state of health evaluates someone’s condition.

items.example: The archive remained in a state of disorder for months.
items.note: Describes serious lack of organisation or order.

items.example: The team remained in a state of uncertainty about funding.
items.note: Uncertainty means a lack of reliable knowledge about outcomes.

items.example: Some families live in a state of poverty despite being employed.
items.note: Poverty is an uncountable social or economic condition.

items.example: The announcement left the audience in a state of agitation.
items.note: Agitation can describe disturbed or anxious excitement.

items.pt: um estado de deterioração; um estado de conservação ruim
items.example: The old station had fallen into a state of disrepair.
items.note: Disrepair means poor condition due to neglect or lack of maintenance.

items.example: The project requirements were still in a state of flux.
items.note: Flux describes continuing change or instability.
